newsitem.title: USA: Watergate's mystery source gets call to come out.
newsitem.headline: Watergate's mystery source gets call to come out.

text.p: A senator who asked the key question at the Watergate hearings called on Sunday for the mystery figure known as "Deep Throat" to unmask himself and throw new light on the 25-year-old scandal that led to Richard Nixon's resignation as president.
Howard Baker, who became a celebrity as vice chairman of the Senate Watergate Committee, said it would be a shame to let "Deep Throat" take his or her secrets to the grave.

"If there is a single person who is 'Deep Throat', it's a shame to wait until he dies and can't speak in order to talk to him," Baker, a Tennessee Republican, said on the NBC programme "Meet the Press."
Deep Throat was the code name of a super-secret source for Bob Woodward's and Carl Bernstein's aggressive Washington Post reporting on Nixon's efforts to thwart investigation of the scandal.
The name came from a 1970s pornographic film and was a play on the phrase "deep background," or confidential information that cannot be attributed to a specific person.

Whoever he was -- Woodward and Bernstein have said it was a man -- Deep Throat fed clues that linked the Nixon White House to a botched break-in at Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate complex 25 years ago this week, on June 17, 1972.

In a discussion pegged to the break-in's anniversary, Benjamin Bradlee, then Woodward and Bernstein's editor, said the reporters planned to unveil Deep Throat's identity once he died. But Bradlee, who is privy to the secret, said Deep Throat could release the Washington Post "from our obligation to not identify him any time he wants."
"Well, that's sort of what I'm suggesting," Baker jumped in, "that he ought to do that so we can find out ... maybe he's listening."
Baker, who said he did not know the source's identity, asked the Watergate hearing's most memorable question: "What did the president know and when did he know it?"

On "Meet the Press", he voiced doubt that the American people would ever know the answer to that question, notably because of the deaths of Nixon and former Attorney General John Mitchell, who served 19 months in prison for conspiracy, obstruction of justice and perjury.
Woodward did not immediately return a telephone message seeking comment on future plans to disclose the secret. Bernstein could not be reached.
Their stories led to the congressional investigation and Nixon's resignation on Aug. 9, 1974, in the face of near certain impeachement by the House of Representatives.

Over the years, speculation about Deep Throat's identity has centred on a handful of top officials, including L. Patrick Gray, then acting director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and Alexander Haig, a former Nixon chief of staff.

Then-White House counsel John Dean, whose testimony at the Watergate hearings hurt Nixon, denied on "Meet the Press" that he was Deep Throat. He said he had concluded that Gray was the one, a notion that Gray has denied.
